title: Suez Crisis
wiki_lead:
The Suez Crisis, also known as the second Arab–Israeli war, the Tripartite Aggression in the Arab world and the Sinai War in Israel, was a British–French–Israeli invasion of Egypt in 1956. Israel invaded on 29 October, with the primary objective of re-opening the Straits of Tiran and the Gulf of Aqaba as the recent tightening of the eight-year-long Egyptian blockade prevented Israeli passage. After issuing a joint ultimatum for a ceasefire, the United Kingdom and France joined the Israelis on 31 October in an attempt to depose Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser and regain control of the Suez Canal (which Nasser had nationalised earlier that year). The countries came under heavy political pressure from the United States, the Soviet Union and the United Nations, prompting their withdrawal from Egypt.
The crisis demonstrated that the United Kingdom and France could no longer implement independent foreign policies without U.S. consent. Israel's four-month-long occupation of the Egyptian-occupied Gaza Strip and Egypt's Sinai Peninsula enabled it to freely navigate the Straits of Tiran, but the Suez Canal was closed from October 1956 to March 1957.
The crisis strengthened Nasser's standing, internationally humiliating the British (as historians questioned its role as a superpower) and the French during the Cold War. The UN established an emergency force to police the Egypt–Israel border. For his diplomatic efforts to resolve the conflict through the UN, Canadian external-affairs minister Lester B. Pearson received the Nobel Peace Prize. Analysts have said that the crisis may have emboldened the USSR, facilitating the Soviet invasion of Hungary.

Background


Before 1945

The Suez Canal opened in 1869, financed by the French and Egyptian governments. The canal was operated by the Suez Company, an Egyptian-chartered company; the area surrounding the canal remained Egyptian territory. The canal was strategically important, as it provided the shortest ocean link between the Mediterranean Sea and the Indian Ocean.
In 1875, as a result of a financial crisis, Egypt sold its shares in the company to the British government. They obtained a 44-percent share in the company for £4 million (equivalent to £399 million in 2025). With the 1882 invasion and occupation of Egypt, the UK took de facto control of the country and the canal. The 1888 Convention of Constantinople declared the canal a neutral zone under British protection, and the Ottoman Empire agreed to permit international shipping to pass freely through the canal.
Despite the convention, Britain closed the canal several times. During the 1904–05 Russo-Japanese War, the British denied the Russian Baltic Fleet use of the canal after the Dogger Bank incident and forced it to sail around Africa (giving the Imperial Japanese Armed Forces time to consolidate their position). grok_lead: The Suez Crisis was a brief but pivotal armed conflict in 1956 in which Israel invaded Egypt's Sinai Peninsula on 29 October, followed by Anglo-French military intervention aimed at regaining control of the Suez Canal after its nationalization by Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser. Nasser's nationalization decree on 26 July expropriated the British- and French-owned Suez Canal Company, which had operated the strategically vital waterway since its opening in 1869, in retaliation for the withdrawal of U.S. and British funding for the Aswan High Dam amid Egypt's overtures to the Soviet bloc for arms and economic ties. Israel 's preemptive strike addressed Egyptian blockades of the Straits of Tiran, which impeded Israeli shipping to the Red Sea, and cross-border fedayeen terrorist raids sponsored by Egypt from Gaza, achieving rapid military successes including the capture of Sharm el-Sheikh and destruction of much of Egypt's air force and armor. Britain and France, seeking to secure their oil supply routes and reverse the erosion of imperial prestige, secretly coordinated with Israel via the SÃ¨vres Protocol to provoke a pretext for intervention: after Israel 's advance, the two powers issued a ceasefire ultimatum to Egypt and Israel, then launched air strikes and amphibious landings to occupy the canal zone on 5 November. The operation exposed vulnerabilities in Western unity during the Cold War, as U.S. President Dwight D. Eisenhower, prioritizing containment of Soviet influence and avoiding perceptions of European colonialism, applied intense economic pressureâincluding threats to withhold oil supplies and IMF supportâwhile the United Nations passed resolutions demanding withdrawal under Canadian-led peacekeeping auspices. Despite tactical victoriesâIsraeli forces routed Egyptian troops in Sinai, and Anglo-French troops secured Port Said âthe invaders faced mounting fuel shortages, Soviet nuclear saber-rattling, and domestic political backlash, forcing a humiliating retreat by March 1957 that left the canal under Egyptian control. The crisis accelerated the decline of British and French great-power status, boosted Nasser's pan-Arab nationalism as a symbol of anti-imperial resistance, temporarily secured Israeli access to southern waters until 1967, and underscored the shift in global hegemony toward U.S. dominance, with lasting disruptions to oil flows exacerbating economic strains in Europe.
